patient.name: Margaret O'Sullivan
patient.complaint: Two days of right upper abdominal pain, fevers with shaking and yellow eyes
background: Known gallstones on ultrasound 2 years ago, awaiting cholecystectomy
Lives with her husband in Kilburn

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with RUQ pain, jaundice and fever (Charcot's triad), with cholecystitis, biliary colic and pancreatitis as distractors. Hypotension and confusion (Reynold's pentad) signal severe disease; E. coli is the classic organism question.

points: Two days of **RUQ pain**; rigors last night.
Husband noticed her **eyes have gone yellow**.

visual.title: Where Margaret's pain is
visual.caption: RUQ pain plus jaundice plus fever: the stone is in the **common bile duct**, not just the gallbladder.

steps.q: Which combination makes this cholangitis rather than cholecystitis?
steps.r: **Charcot's triad**: RUQ pain, jaundice and fever. Cholecystitis rarely causes jaundice because the duct is not blocked.

steps.lead: Margaret has the full **Charcot's triad** and visible scleral icterus.
Margaret's bile is infected behind an obstruction: almost certainly a **stone in her CBD** (choledocholithiasis), with E. coli the likely culprit.
Her known **gallstones** are the risk factor. A previous ERCP or biliary surgery would also count.

points: Four hours later Margaret is **confused**, GCS 14.
BP falls to 86/50 mmHg despite a fluid bolus.

steps.lead: Hypotension and confusion on top of Charcot's triad: **Reynold's pentad**. Margaret is now septic.
Without decompression Margaret risks **hepatic abscess**, gallbladder empyema, sepsis and multi-organ failure.

steps.text: Fever + RUQ pain **without jaundice** suggests cholecystitis. Add jaundice and it is cholangitis until proven otherwise.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (abdominal ultrasound) and recognising the cholestatic blood picture; MRCP is the most accurate non-invasive test, and ERCP is the gold standard because it also treats.

steps.title: Margaret's bloods
steps.text: Raised inflammatory markers plus a **cholestatic** pattern (ALP and GGT far higher than ALT).

steps.lead: Margaret's raised **CRP and WCC** with high bilirubin and ALP is the classic picture. **Ultrasound** is the first scan.

visual.title: Bilirubin
visual.label: Margaret 98
visual.caption: Jaundice is usually visible in the sclerae once bilirubin is above about 40–50.

points: Bedside ultrasound: **dilated CBD (11 mm)** and intrahepatic ducts.
Distal CBD poorly seen behind bowel gas.

steps.q: The ultrasound cannot see the distal duct. Which test best delineates it without an invasive procedure?
steps.r: **MRCP** is the most accurate non-invasive imaging. ERCP is invasive (and therapeutic).

steps.lead: Margaret's MRCP confirms a **12 mm stone in the distal CBD**, mapping the obstruction before ERCP.
**ERCP** is the gold standard because it both confirms the stone and removes it in the same procedure.

steps.text: Do not send a septic patient for MRCP before resuscitation and antibiotics. Bloods, cultures and ultrasound first.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' (ABCDE, sepsis bundle, IV co-amoxiclav) and 'definitive management' (ERCP within 24–48 hours; PTBD if ERCP is not possible). Penicillin allergy changes the antibiotic.

steps.title: Margaret's first hour
steps.caption: Sepsis bundle first: decompression follows once she is resuscitated.

steps.q: Margaret has no allergies. Which antibiotic is first-line?
steps.r: **IV co-amoxiclav** first-line. Ciprofloxacin plus metronidazole (or cefuroxime) is for penicillin allergy.

steps.lead: Margaret gets **antibiotics plus a plan for biliary decompression**: ABCDE, fluids, oxygen, monitoring and IV co-amoxiclav.
Once stabilised, Margaret has **ERCP** the next morning: sphincterotomy and stone extraction. If ERCP were impossible, **PTBD** would drain her ducts.

visual.title: Before and after ERCP
visual.caption: Fever and bilirubin fall quickly once the duct is decompressed.

steps.lead: Margaret's care follows NICE gallstone guidance and the **Tokyo Guidelines** for grading and managing cholangitis.

steps.text: Antibiotics alone rarely cure cholangitis: the **obstruction must be relieved**. Once settled, Margaret is listed for cholecystectomy to prevent recurrence.
Emergency open surgery is not the first decompression. ERCP (or PTBD) drains the duct with far less risk in a septic patient.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why obstruction leads to infection (stasis plus ascending enteric organisms such as E. coli), why sepsis follows (raised biliary pressure), why jaundice and ALP rise, and why ERCP fixes it.

steps.lead: Margaret's impacted CBD stone caused **bile stasis**; gut bacteria such as E. coli then ascended and infected it.

steps.title: From stone to septic shock
nodes: Bacteria and toxins translocate into blood

steps.lead: Margaret's rising duct pressure pushed bacteria into her bloodstream: her hypotension and confusion were **septic shock and encephalopathy**.
Conjugated bilirubin could not drain, so it spilled into her blood: **jaundice**, dark urine and pale stools, with raised **ALP and GGT**.
Margaret's ERCP removed the stone, dropping the pressure and stopping further **bacterial translocation**.

steps.text: Conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble, so it appears in urine (dark). Less reaches the gut, so stools are pale.

mcq.q: What are the components of Charcot's triad?
o: Hypotension, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds

mcq.q: Which two features does Reynold's pentad add?
mcq.r: **Hypotension and confusion**: severe disease and sepsis.

mcq.q: What is the most common cause of acute cholangitis?
What is the first-line radiological investigation?
What is the most accurate non-invasive imaging?
Why is ERCP the gold standard?
Which type of bilirubin rises in cholangitis?

technique.stem: A 68 year old woman has a 2 day history of right upper quadrant pain and shaking chills. She has known gallstones. Her temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 110 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg. Her sclerae are yellow. Murphy's sign is negative.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about RUQ pain: is there fever and is there jaundice?
RUQ pain + fever + jaundice = **Charcot's triad**; known stones; cholestatic bloods.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Infected obstructed CBD: **acute cholangitis**.

elim: Cholecystitis gives fever and RUQ pain but rarely jaundice.
Pancreatitis gives epigastric pain to the back with raised amylase.
Biliary colic has no fever or jaundice.
Hepatitis A gives a hepatitic pattern (high ALT), not ALP-led cholestasis.

steps.x: **A. Acute cholangitis.** Charcot's triad = cholangitis.

technique.stem: A 71 year old man has fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain. He has been given IV fluids, blood cultures have been taken and IV co-amoxiclav started. His temperature is 38.5°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial radiological investigation?

steps.x: The **initial radiological** test, not the gold standard.

clues: fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain
steps.x: Charcot's triad, resuscitation underway; now image.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Abdominal ultrasound**: quick, bedside, shows dilated ducts and stones.

elim: CT is less sensitive for gallstones; not first-line.
ERCP is the gold standard and treatment, not the first scan.
HIDA is for cholecystitis when ultrasound is equivocal.
MRCP is second-line, to delineate the obstruction.

steps.x: **E. Ultrasound.** Then MRCP, then ERCP.

technique.stem: A 66 year old woman with acute cholangitis has been resuscitated and given IV co-amoxiclav. MRCP shows a stone in the common bile duct. She had a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass 5 years ago, so the endoscopist cannot reach the papilla. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 108 bpm and BP 100/64 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?

steps.x: Definitive management when the usual route is blocked.

clues: stone in the common bile duct
steps.x: Still septic, needs decompression, ERCP not possible.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage**.

elim: Antibiotics alone do not relieve the obstruction.
Cholecystectomy removes the gallbladder, not a CBD stone, and 6 weeks is too late.
ERCP is first choice but cannot be done here.
Ursodeoxycholic acid does not treat an infected obstruction.

steps.x: **D. PTBD.** ERCP within 24–48 h; if unsuitable, PTBD.

technique.stem: A 70 year old man has acute cholangitis due to a stone in the common bile duct. He reports dark urine and pale stools. His temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his dark urine?
o: Unconjugated bilirubin filtered by the kidney

steps.x: A mechanism question: why is the urine dark?

clues: stone in the common bile duct
steps.x: Obstructive picture: bilirubin is conjugated but cannot drain.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Water-soluble **conjugated bilirubin** is excreted by the kidney.

elim: Haemolysis gives unconjugated bilirubin and no pale stools.
Urobilinogen falls in obstruction because less bilirubin reaches the gut.
No muscle injury here.
Unconjugated bilirubin is albumin-bound and not filtered.

steps.x: **D.** Obstruction = conjugated bilirubin in urine, little in stool.

practice.stem: A 79 year old man has a 3 day history of right upper quadrant pain and fevers. His wife says his eyes look yellow. He has known gallstones. His temperature is 39.0°C, pulse rate 114 bpm, BP 112/68 mmHg and respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: RUQ pain, fever and jaundice (Charcot's triad) with a cholestatic, inflammatory blood picture is acute cholangitis. Cholecystitis rarely causes jaundice.

steps.x: Diagnosis of RUQ pain with systemic features.

clues: right upper quadrant pain and fevers
steps.x: Charcot's triad with cholestatic LFTs and high WCC.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Acute cholangitis**.

elim: Cholecystitis: fever and RUQ pain, usually no jaundice.
Biliary colic: no fever, no jaundice.
Liver abscess is a complication; jaundice is uncommon.
Pancreatic cancer gives painless jaundice and weight loss.

steps.x: **A.** Charcot's triad = cholangitis.

practice.stem: A 64 year old woman has fever, rigors, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain. Ultrasound shows a dilated common bile duct. She has never had biliary surgery or endoscopy. Her temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 106 bpm and BP 120/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her condition?
practice.e: Choledocholithiasis (stones in the CBD) is by far the most common cause of acute cholangitis. Malignant obstruction usually presents with painless jaundice.

steps.x: A 'most likely cause' question: what is blocking the duct?
Cholangitis with an obstructed CBD and no previous instrumentation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Choledocholithiasis**.

elim: Strictures follow surgery or ERCP; she has had neither.
Cholangiocarcinoma is rarer and gives painless jaundice and weight loss.
Pancreatic cancer gives painless jaundice.
PSC is a chronic disease linked to ulcerative colitis.

steps.x: **C.** Gallstones in the CBD are by far the commonest cause.

practice.stem: A 72 year old man is admitted with right upper quadrant pain, jaundice and fever. Blood cultures grow a Gram-negative rod that ferments lactose. He has gallstones. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 110 bpm and BP 108/66 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: E. coli, a lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rod from the gut, is a common cause of ascending cholangitis.

steps.x: An organism question.
Ascending biliary infection; lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rod.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **E. coli**.

elim: Clostridium is a Gram-positive rod.
Enterococcus is a Gram-positive coccus.
S. aureus is a Gram-positive coccus.
S. pneumoniae is a Gram-positive diplococcus.

steps.x: **C. E. coli.** Ascending enteric organisms.

practice.stem: A 58 year old woman had an ERCP for a common bile duct stent change 2 days ago. She now has right upper quadrant pain, rigors and worsening jaundice. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and BP 110/70 mmHg. Her abdomen is soft with RUQ tenderness only.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Cholangitis is a known complication of ERCP; Charcot's triad with normal amylase makes it more likely than post-ERCP pancreatitis.

steps.x: A diagnosis question after ERCP.
Charcot's triad after biliary instrumentation; normal amylase.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Post-ERCP **acute cholangitis**.

elim: Pancreatitis would raise amylase; it is normal.
Perforation gives peritonism and free air; abdomen is soft.
Bleeding gives melaena and falling Hb, not rigors.
Colic has no fever.

steps.x: **A.** ERCP is a known cause of cholangitis.

practice.stem: A 76 year old woman with acute cholangitis has deteriorated. She is now drowsy and disorientated with a GCS of 14. Her temperature is 39.2°C, pulse rate 128 bpm and BP 82/48 mmHg despite 1 L of IV fluid.
practice.q: Which is the most likely explanation for her deterioration?
o: Reynold's pentad: septic shock from cholangitis
practice.e: Hypotension and confusion added to Charcot's triad form Reynold's pentad, reflecting septic shock and encephalopathy from severe cholangitis.

steps.x: Which explanation fits the new confusion and hypotension?
Charcot's triad + hypotension + confusion.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Reynold's pentad**: septic shock.

elim: Hepatic encephalopathy needs liver failure, not acute sepsis.
Hypoglycaemia does not cause fluid-refractory hypotension.
Stroke gives focal signs and does not explain shock.
Wernicke's needs alcohol or malnutrition, with ataxia and ophthalmoplegia.

steps.x: **C. Reynold's pentad.** Severe cholangitis, urgent decompression.

practice.stem: A 69 year old man was treated for acute cholangitis with antibiotics but declined ERCP. Two weeks later he has swinging fevers, right upper quadrant pain and weight loss. His temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg. Ultrasound shows a 6 cm fluid-filled cavity in the right lobe of the liver.
practice.q: Which is the most likely complication?
practice.e: Untreated cholangitis can lead to a hepatic abscess: swinging fevers and a fluid-filled liver cavity after inadequately treated biliary infection.

steps.x: A complication question after untreated obstruction.

clues: fluid-filled cavity in the right lobe of the liver
steps.x: Obstruction not relieved; swinging fever; liver collection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Hepatic abscess**.

elim: Perforation gives peritonitis, not a liver cavity.
HCC is a solid mass, usually in cirrhosis.
Hydatid needs exposure to dogs or sheep; daughter cysts.
Simple cysts do not cause fevers.

steps.x: **B.** Untreated cholangitis: abscess, empyema, sepsis, MOF.

practice.stem: A 74 year old woman has right upper quadrant pain, jaundice and fever. She has been resuscitated and given IV co-amoxiclav. Her temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial radiological investigation?
practice.e: Abdominal ultrasound is the first-line radiological investigation, showing dilated bile ducts and gallstones.

steps.x: The **first-line** scan.
Charcot's triad, being treated; image the biliary tree.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Abdominal ultrasound**.

elim: CT is not first-line for biliary stones.
ERCP is the gold standard and treatment, not the first scan.
MRCP is second-line.
AXR misses most gallstones.

steps.x: **A. Ultrasound.**

practice.stem: A 67 year old man with suspected acute cholangitis has an abdominal ultrasound showing a dilated common bile duct of 12 mm, but the distal duct is obscured by bowel gas and no stone is seen. He is improving on antibiotics. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation to delineate the obstruction?
practice.e: MRCP is the most accurate non-invasive imaging and is used to confirm the diagnosis and delineate the obstruction before ERCP.

steps.x: Next test to delineate the obstruction when ultrasound is inconclusive.
Dilated duct, cause unseen, patient stable.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **MRCP**.

elim: CT is less accurate for duct stones.
EUS is invasive; MRCP is the standard non-invasive test.
HIDA assesses cystic duct patency (cholecystitis).
Waiting 6 weeks risks recurrent sepsis.

steps.x: **D. MRCP**, then ERCP.

practice.stem: A 70 year old woman has right upper quadrant pain, jaundice and fever. Her temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 116 bpm, BP 98/60 mmHg and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. She has no drug allergies. Blood cultures have been taken.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Septic cholangitis needs ABCDE and sepsis management with IV fluids and IV co-amoxiclav first, then biliary decompression by ERCP.

steps.x: Initial management of septic cholangitis.
Septic, cultures done, no allergy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV fluids and IV co-amoxiclav**, then ERCP.

elim: Cholecystectomy does not clear the CBD and is risky in sepsis.
Oral treatment at home is unsafe in sepsis.
Ursodeoxycholic acid does nothing for infected obstruction.
Antibiotics must not wait for imaging.

steps.x: **B.** Sepsis bundle with IV co-amoxiclav first.

practice.stem: A 63 year old man has acute cholangitis. He had anaphylaxis to penicillin 10 years ago. His temperature is 38.5°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. IV fluids have been started.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic regimen?
practice.e: With penicillin allergy, cholangitis is treated with IV ciprofloxacin plus metronidazole (or IV cefuroxime). Co-amoxiclav and pip-taz contain penicillins.

steps.x: Antibiotic choice: check the allergy.
Cholangitis but co-amoxiclav is contraindicated.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV ciprofloxacin plus metronidazole**.

elim: Co-amoxiclav contains amoxicillin.
Pip-taz is a penicillin.
Amoxicillin is a penicillin and oral.
Nitrofurantoin is for lower UTI only.

steps.x: **A.** Penicillin allergy: cipro + metronidazole.

practice.stem: A 77 year old woman with acute cholangitis has been resuscitated and is on IV co-amoxiclav for 12 hours. Her temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 116/70 mmHg. MRCP shows a 10 mm stone in the distal common bile duct.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
practice.e: Definitive management is ERCP within 24–48 hours to relieve the obstruction (sphincterotomy and stone extraction). Antibiotics alone do not decompress the duct.

steps.x: **Definitive** management of the obstruction.

clues: stone in the distal common bile duct
steps.x: Stabilised, stone confirmed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **ERCP within 24–48 hours**.

elim: Antibiotics alone leave the obstruction.
ESWL is not standard for CBD stones.
Open exploration is higher risk than ERCP.
Ursodeoxycholic acid does not clear a CBD stone.

steps.x: **B. ERCP.** PTBD if ERCP is unsuitable.

practice.stem: A 73 year old man with a stone impacted in the common bile duct develops rigors, confusion and a BP of 84/50 mmHg. His pulse rate is 124 bpm. Blood cultures grow E. coli. After ERCP decompression his BP recovers within hours.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his bacteraemia?
o: Haematogenous spread from a urinary tract infection
Raised biliary pressure causing bacterial translocation into the blood
Spread from the portal vein to the gut
Transmural spread through the duodenal wall
practice.e: Rising pressure in the obstructed biliary tree allows bacteria and toxins to translocate into the bloodstream, causing bacteraemia and sepsis; decompression stops this.

steps.x: A mechanism question: how do bacteria reach the blood?

clues: stone impacted in the common bile duct
steps.x: Obstruction, bacteraemia, rapid improvement once pressure is relieved.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Raised biliary pressure** pushes bacteria into the blood.

elim: No urinary source; ERCP fixed it.
Lymphatic spread does not explain rapid recovery after decompression.
Bacteria ascend from the gut into bile, not from portal vein to gut.
Transmural spread is not the mechanism.

steps.x: **C.** Obstruction → pressure → translocation; ERCP stops it.

glossary.Cholangitis: Infection of the bile ducts, usually behind an obstruction.
glossary.Choledocholithiasis: Gallstones in the common bile duct.
glossary.CBD: Common bile duct, carrying bile from the liver and gallbladder to the duodenum.
glossary.Charcot's triad: RUQ pain, jaundice and fever: the classic presentation of cholangitis.
glossary.Reynold's pentad: Charcot's triad plus hypotension and confusion: severe cholangitis with sepsis.
glossary.Scleral icterus: Yellowing of the whites of the eyes from raised bilirubin.
glossary.Jaundice: Yellow skin and eyes from raised bilirubin.
glossary.Rigors: Uncontrollable shaking with fever, suggesting bacteraemia.
glossary.ERCP: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography: endoscope into the bile duct to diagnose and remove stones.
glossary.MRCP: MRI of the bile and pancreatic ducts; the most accurate non-invasive biliary imaging.
glossary.Sphincterotomy: Cutting the sphincter of Oddi at ERCP to let stones out.
glossary.PTBD: Percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage: a drain through the liver into the ducts when ERCP is not possible.
glossary.Percutaneous transhepatic biliary draina: Draining the bile ducts through the skin and liver under imaging guidance.
glossary.Cholestasis: Reduced bile flow, causing raised conjugated bilirubin, ALP and GGT.
glossary.Conjugated bilirubin: Water-soluble bilirubin processed by the liver; appears in urine when bile is blocked.
glossary.ALP: Alkaline phosphatase; rises in bile duct obstruction.
glossary.GGT: Gamma-glutamyl transferase; rises with ALP in cholestasis.
glossary.ALT: Alanine aminotransferase; a marker of liver cell damage.
glossary.Biliary colic: Pain from a stone transiently blocking the gallbladder outlet, without fever or jaundice.
glossary.Cholecystitis: Inflammation of the gallbladder from an impacted stone, with pain and fever but usually no jaundice.
glossary.Murphy's sign: Pain and a catch of breath on palpating the RUQ during inspiration; suggests cholecystitis.
glossary.Hepatic abscess: A collection of pus within the liver.
glossary.Translocation: Movement of bacteria or toxins from one compartment (bile) into the blood.
glossary.Septic shock: Sepsis with hypotension needing vasopressors and a high lactate.
glossary.Co-amoxiclav: Amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid; first-line IV antibiotic for cholangitis.
glossary.Metronidazole: Antibiotic covering anaerobes; used with ciprofloxacin in penicillin allergy.
glossary.Tokyo Guidelines: International criteria for diagnosing and grading acute cholangitis and cholecystitis.
glossary.E. coli: Escherichia coli, a Gram-negative gut bacterium and common cause of cholangitis.
glossary.Cholecystectomy: Surgical removal of the gallbladder, offered after recovery to prevent recurrence.
